extracted.intended_audience: general educated Victorian magazine readers (readers of Temple Bar / Chambers’s Journal / Cornhill Magazine)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting prescriptive customs, ritual rules, and technical recommendations from a mixed Victorian magazine excerpt (folk customs, funeral rites, and an essay on electricity/gas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wedding-omen: slips/falls/accidents as bad augury
rubrics_metrics.description: If the bride or one of the bridal party slips by the way, if the ring or one of the candles on the altar falls in church, the young couple may look out for sorrow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text states these incidents are traditionally read as portentous of future sorrow for the couple.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wedding-omen: two sisters married same day
rubrics_metrics.description: If two sisters are married on the same day, ill will fare the younger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local belief presented as a rule about relative fortune when siblings wed the same day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wedding-omen: asymmetry in candles or rising
rubrics_metrics.description: If one candle shines with less brilliancy than the other, or one of the kneeling spouses rises before the other, that one whose candle has not burnt as it should, or the one who has risen before the partner, will die first or die soon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A paired-symbolity rule: imbalance in ritual elements is interpreted as an omen of early death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Piano de’ Greci nuptial headwear custom
rubrics_metrics.description: In Piano de’ Greci—the young husband keeps his Phrygian cap on his head in church, as a sign that he too is now the head of a new family; and in olden times the bride used to come into church on horseback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes prescriptive local signifiers of marital status (what the husband/bride wear or how she enters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Salaparuta marriage-door and campanile requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: In one place, Salaparuta, the bride enters in at the small door and goes out by the large; and she must perforce pass beneath the campanile, else she has not been married properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strict procedural requirement for a valid/local marriage ritual: specified sequence of entry/exit and physical passage beneath the bell-tower.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sicilian-Albanian wedding ritual sequence (rings, crowns, priest veil, triple feeding, broken glass, dance, hymns, Holy Kiss)
rubrics_metrics.description: After the wedding-rings—of gold for the man, of silver for the woman—the officiating priest puts a white veil on himself, steeps some bread in a glass of wine, and gives the young couple to eat three times; after which, invoking the name of the Lord, he dashes the glass to the ground. Then they all dance a certain decorous (three turns) dance guided by the priest, with the accompaniment of two hymns (one to Isaiah, the other 'Absit omen' to the Holy Martyrs). After the dance comes the Holy Kiss: the priest kisses the husband only, and he kisses all the men and his bride; she kisses only all the women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full procedural description of ritual actions, materials (gold/silver rings), symbolic feedings and gendered order of kisses—presented as the correct ceremonial sequence in those colonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-ceremony throwing/gifts and symbolic meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: On their return from church 'confetti' are thrown before the newly-married couple; or boxes of sweetmeats are given. In places they throw dried peas, beans, almonds and corn (corn = sign of plenty). Variations include vegetables, bread and corn and salt mixed; corn and nuts; or 'dolci' made of wheaten flour and honey. In Syracuse they throw salt (symbol of wisdom) and wheat (symbol of plenty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes acceptable post-ceremony tokens to cast or distribute and their conventional symbolic meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avola entrance/egg-and-leaves rites
rubrics_metrics.description: In Avola, the nearest neighbor goes up to the bride with an apron full of orange leaves, which she flings in her face, saying, 'Continence and boy-children!' then strews the remainder before the house-door. To this ceremony is added breaking two hen’s eggs at the feet of the 'sposi.' In one place they sprinkle the threshold with wine before entering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local prescribed actions and spoken formulae at the bride’s first entrance—presented as required or customary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mother-in-law spoonful-honey welcome and ciambelle
rubrics_metrics.description: At Piano de’ Greci and in the other Sicilian-Greek colonies, the mother-in-law stands at the door of the house waiting for her daughter-in-law to give her a spoonful of honey as soon as she enters, to which are added 'ciambelle'—small ring-shaped cakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies an expected exchange/gift ritual between bride and mother-in-law at house-entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bride’s-house adornment and omen of crossed wire
rubrics_metrics.description: The bride’s house is adorned with flowers, but it is a bad omen if two bits of wire get put by chance crosswise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive décor practice with a specific superstition about accidental crossed wires being an ill omen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-wedding social procedures (dining, seating, invitations, receptions, dancing, bridal chamber escort, contracted entitlements)
rubrics_metrics.description: At dinner the bridegroom leaves the bride to go to his own home, but he returns in the middle of the meal to finish it with his bride. They are very particular as to who shall sit on the right and who on the left of the bride. The first day of receptions all the invitations are given by the mother of the bride; the second day by the mother of the bridegroom. A plate is set to receive contributions (Penny Weddings). In the evening they dance: the 'sposo' cap in hand bows to the bride, she dances, then the 'zitu' bows and sits; the bride dances alone once then selects partners. Songs and dances finished, the mother-in-law accompanies the bride to the bride-chamber; if absent this devolves on the bridegroom’s married sister or nearest relation. The bride stays eight days receiving visits and later goes to church dressed all in white. The marriage contract may specify to what festas and amusements the husband shall take her and even the number of dishes and dresses allowed during the year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combines multiple prescriptive social conventions and contractual specifications governing ceremonies, hospitality, and post-nuptial domestic entitlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance threshold: practical jokes and social impropriety
rubrics_metrics.description: Often all sorts of rude practical jokes are played, especially on old people or second marriages; some of which are horribly unseemly, and all are inconvenient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes social norm disapproval—such joking is treated as improper though commonplace; guidance is implicitly to avoid such unseemly practical jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viaticum and prognostications of death
rubrics_metrics.description: Among old Sicilian rules was one which enjoined, after three days’ illness, the Viaticum. The most common prognostications of death are: the midnight howling of a dog; the hooting of an owl; the crowing of a hen at midnight; to dream of dead friends or kinsfolk; to sweep the house at night; or to make a new opening of any kind in an inhabited house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies when the Last Sacraments (Viaticum) are expected and lists omens traditionally read as signs of imminent death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responses when death delays (ritual actions to hasten/avert)
rubrics_metrics.description: If delayed, something supernatural is suspected. If he delays his dying, the friends must call out his name in seven Litanies, or at least put his clothes out of doors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescribes remedial or ritual actions to be taken when death does not occur when expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corpse-preparation and mourner behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: When he dies the women raise the death-howl and let loose their hair about their shoulders. All his good qualities are enumerated and his bad ones are forgotten. He is dressed in white, and after he is dressed his shroud is sewn tight (the needle is preserved as sacred or buried with the corpse). Sometimes women are buried in their wedding-dress. The corpse is always laid out feet foremost to the door. About the corpse-bed stand lighted candles or at least one little oil lamp. The hired mourners ('repulatrici') tear their hair and throw it in handfuls on the corpse; sisters lament in mournful songs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed prescriptive practices for preparing the body, rites of lamentation, and material arrangements at the corpse-bed; includes preservation of ritual implements as sacred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mourning durations by relation
rubrics_metrics.description: The mourning lasts one or two years for parents, husband or wife, and brothers and sisters; six months for grandparents, and uncles and aunts; three months for a cousin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives explicit canonical durations for public mourning according to family relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infant burial protocol and public response
rubrics_metrics.description: Babies are buried in white with a red ribbon as a sash, or disposed over the body in the form of a cross. They lie in a basket on the table with wax candles set round, and their faces are covered with a fine veil. No one must weep for the death of an infant; the announcement of its death is received with a cry of 'Glory and Paradise!' and in some places the joybells are rung as for a festa. When taken to the Campo Santo, it is accompanied with music and singing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescribes a markedly different set of rites and public affect (joyful acceptance) for infants, with specified material arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Afterlife-soul-manifestation beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul of the dead is to be seen as a butterfly, a dove, an angel. The soul of a murdered man hovers about the cross raised to his memory on the place of his murder; the soul of one righteously executed by the law remains on earth to frighten the timid; the soul of the suicide goes plumb to hell unless he repents at the supreme moment. Judas is condemned to hover always over the 'tamarix Gallica'; children go to the stars; certain women believe their souls will go up the 'stairs of St. Japicu di Galizia' (the Milky Way).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catalogues culturally specific cosmological expectations about post-mortem appearances and destinations—informing ritual interpretation and behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funeral/bridal intersection taboo and averting practices
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the worst possible omen for a bridal procession to meet a funeral. It has to be averted by making the 'horns' (thrusting the thumb between the first two fingers) or by putting a pomegranate before the door or in the window.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies taboo and concrete apotropaic gestures/objects used to avert the ill omen of a funeral meeting a wedding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community funeral provisioning and household signals
rubrics_metrics.description: At Piano de’ Greci certain little loaves or bread-cakes in the form of a cross are given to the poor on the day of a death. In Giacosa, behind the funeral procession comes an ass laden with food which, after the burial, is distributed. The Sicilian-Albanians do not sit on chairs during the first days of mourning, but on the dead man’s mattress. In some houses all is thrown into intentional confusion—turned upside down—to mark the presence of death; others put out the mattress to show the invalid is dead; others remake the bed as for marriage placing on it the crucifix which the sick man had held when dying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encompasses communal and household behaviors that signal death and orchestrate distribution of food/charity; offers concrete alternative household practices tied to mourning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electric Lighting Act: licensing and supply conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Electric Lighting Act authorizes the Board of Trade to grant licences to Companies and local authorities to supply electricity under certain conditions. These conditions have reference chiefly to the limits of compulsory and permissive supply, the securing of a regular and efficient supply, the safety of the public, the limitation of prices to be charged, and regulations as to inspection and inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal regulatory criteria for authorized electric supply—limits of supply, service regularity, public safety, price limits, and inspection/regulatory oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of electric lighting and present practical choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Lighting may be effected in one of three ways—(1) by primary batteries; (2) by dynamo-machines; or (3) by a combination of dynamo machines and secondary batteries. The expense of working with primary batteries is altogether prohibitory except for very small installations; secondary batteries have not yet been made a practical success; so that the second method (dynamo-machines) is the only one at present in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical recommendation about technology choice: use dynamo-machines for any substantial installation; reserve primary batteries to trivial/small cases; treat secondary batteries as not yet practical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative-cost principle: compare like-for-like scales (central stations vs gas-works)
rubrics_metrics.description: A distinction must be made between isolated installations and a general system of lighting from central stations. It is manifestly unfair to compare cost of electric light from isolated installations with gas obtained from gas-works supplying many thousands of lights. Central stations supplying at least, say, ten thousand lights, and gas-works on an equal scale, must be compared to arrive at a true estimate of relative cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating economic competitiveness, compare systems on equal operational scale (central-station electricity vs large gasworks), not isolated one-off setups vs mass gas supply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incandescent lighting advantages and best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The incandescent light is free from products of combustion which heat and vitiate the air; it enables us to see pictures and flowers as by daylight; it supports plants instead of poisoning them; almost perfect immunity from danger of fire and no fear of explosion. A gas flame gives out seventeen times as much heat as an incandescent lamp of equal light-giving power, and an ordinary gas flame vitiates the air as much as the breathing of ten persons. The electric light readily adapts to interior fittings and decorations, should avoid old lines of gas-fittings, and the lights should be placed singly where required and not 'bunched' together. For lighting of mines, electricity stands unrivalled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists sanitary, conservation, safety, and aesthetic advantages of incandescent lighting and prescribes installation best-practices (single strategically-placed lamps; avoid old gas lines) and priority application areas (theatres, mines, showrooms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Electricity as combined power-and-light supply (central plant economy)
rubrics_metrics.description: With the general introduction of electricity for lighting comes the introduction for production of power; the same current entering by the same conductors can be used for light or power, or both. The same plant at central stations will supply power by day and light by night. Electricity will thus be used for driving sewing-machines, grinding, mixing, brushing, cleaning, and many other domestic purposes. In many trades requiring light machinery for short periods, electricity will be of greatest value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational recommendation: adopt central-station electricity to serve dual needs (daytime power, nighttime light) and for short-duty-cycle industrial/domestic machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projected role of gas: fuel and power producer (not obsolescence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is electricity to supersede gas altogether? By no means. Gas is destined to play a more important part in the future as a fuel and power producer. When gas is burned in an ordinary gas flame, 95% of the gas is consumed in producing heat and 5% only in producing light. Gas-engines are far more economical than steam-engines; it may be advantageous to place gas-works at the colliery and convey gas in pipes to towns. With substitution of gas for coal as fuel will end smoke and wasteful production of smuts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positioning guidance for future energy systems: develop gas for heating and engine-driven power; consider colocating gasworks at coal sources and piping gas to users to reduce smoke and improve urban sanitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lighting-design advisory: avoid bunching, use color effects, and fresh fittings
rubrics_metrics.description: The electric light offers unusual facilities for producing spectacular effects (green, red, white lamps). The old lines of gas-fittings should be avoided where possible, and the lights placed singly where required and not 'bunched' together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical interior-design recommendations for electric lighting: exploit color-capability for theatrical/spectacular effects; redesign fittings rather than retrofit old gas fixtures; prefer discrete lamp placement over clusters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy-storage and alternative-generation caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: The winds, waterfalls, tides, and the motion of the waves are potential future energy sources. Before these can be used to any extent, means must be devised for storing energy in the form of electricity; a problem being vigorously attacked but as yet without much practical success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical caveat: development of storage technology is a prerequisite for effective use of intermittent/natural power sources (tides/waves); suggests research priority.
